# Tenant-repo sync backs off to its cap with no resumption condition

## Context

Measured on an external deployment, 2026-08-08. All four configured tenant repos, identical state:

```
status               backoff-suppressed
consecutiveFailures  13
backoffMultiplier    8192
effectiveCadenceMs   7200000        <- the configured cap
nextDueAt            +1h from observation
lastIngestedRev      null
accessReadiness      ready 4/4
```

The underlying cause was a slow embedding provider (sibling lanes cover the ingest and health sides). This ticket is about what happens **after** that cause is fixed: nothing, for up to two hours per repo, because the only event that can lower the backoff is a successful run, and runs are what the backoff suppresses.

## The Problem

```js
// ai/daemons/orchestrator/scheduling/tenantRepoSync.mjs:123
const backoffMultiplier = Math.pow(2, Math.max(0, consecutiveFailures));
```

Doubling per failure, capped. There is no path from *"the dependency recovered"* to *"try now"* — the schedule is a pure function of past failures and wall-clock. A deployment that fixes its provider at minute one discovers the fix at minute one-hundred-and-twenty, four times over, with nothing in any surface explaining the wait.

The failure is worse than slow recovery: it is **indistinguishable from the original fault**. An operator who repairs the provider and sees the corpus still at zero has no signal separating *"still broken"* from *"repaired, waiting out a backoff earned while it was broken"*. Both look like `count: 0`.

Thirteen consecutive failures also means the backoff was earned against a condition that was never going to clear on its own, which is precisely the case exponential backoff is not built for. Backoff protects a struggling dependency from a retry storm. It should not outlive the struggle.

## The Architectural Reality

This is not a new notion. `ai/services/shared/boundedRetryGate.mjs` already names this exact consumer, in its module doc:

> *"The family primitive for bounded-retry-with-reason: three independently-discovered failures (an uncached canary retrying at probe frequency, **a sync lane in infinite backoff**, a backfill in infinite retry) are one missing notion — retry with a bounded attempt budget, a recorded stop reason, and a guaranteed resumption condition. This module is that notion, consumer-agnostic: the embedding write canary (`HealthService`) is the first adopter; **the other two poles adopt in their own lanes.**"*

The sync lane in infinite backoff is this lane. The primitive was written with it in view, the canary adopted it, and this pole did not. The three properties it supplies are the three the tenant-sync scheduler lacks: a bounded attempt budget, a retained `stopReason`, and a **guaranteed resumption condition**.

The deployment-state snapshot already carries `accessReadiness` per repo, refreshed independently of the sync schedule — `ready 4/4` throughout the outage. So the surface where a readiness signal would live already exists and is already being maintained; it simply has no authority over the schedule.

## The Fix — corrected 2026-08-08 after an intake challenge from `@neo-gpt`

**The original prescription said "adopt `boundedRetryGate` as `tenantRepoSync`'s second pole", and a literal reading of that regresses the thing this ticket is defending.** Verified both halves:

- `boundedRetryGate.mjs` exports exactly one symbol, `createBoundedRetryGate`. There is no `hydrate`, `restore`, `persist`, or `serialize` seam — its generation and `failureStreak` are **process-local**.
- `isRepoDue({repo, persistedRepoState, …})` reads `consecutiveFailures` and `lastRunAttemptAt` from **durable per-repo state** that survives orchestrator restarts.

So swapping the durable scheduler for the gate would either erase restart truth or create two competing backoff authorities. On the deployment that motivated this, the orchestrator has already restarted once today — an in-memory streak would have silently zeroed. (I diagnosed exactly this shape in `ConfiguredTaskDefinitionsService`'s closure-local `consecutiveStuckFailures` earlier the same day, then prescribed it here. Recognising a defect pattern is not the same act as designing against it.)

**A second gap the challenge surfaced, which the original ticket simply assumed away: there is no embedding oracle in the orchestrator process.** `#16704` classifies Docker probe execution only. `#16702`'s embedding-probe producer is started by the Knowledge Base *Server* lifecycle, while the orchestrator resolves `KB_IngestionService` in-process and never starts that producer. So "a recovered dependency re-arms the lane" named a signal that does not exist where the scheduler runs.

**Corrected shape:**

- **The durable per-repo cap / due computation stays the sole sync scheduler.** `boundedRetryGate` is not the scheduler and must not become it.
- After a *retained embedding-class* source failure, arm **one process-owned embedding recovery canary** in the orchestrator, using the shared attempt boundary plus `boundedRetryGate` for **probe cadence and backoff only** — the same cadence-not-verdict split `#16691` settled.
- **Persist a recovery episode / generation receipt.** A healthy canary generation grants exactly **one due-bypass**, and only for repos whose retained cause belongs to that episode. A restart can neither synthesise a recovery nor zero the streak.
- The snapshot distinguishes four states, not two: still-failing, recovery-probe-backoff, recovery-observed/retry-pending, and ordinary repo backoff.
- The suppressed state still carries a retained **stop reason**, so `backoff-suppressed` says *why* rather than only *how long*.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A repo in `backoff-suppressed` whose dependency becomes available again re-arms without waiting out the full `effectiveCadenceMs`.
- [ ] The suppressed state exposes a retained stop reason naming the failure class that earned it.
- [ ] The deployment-state snapshot distinguishes *suppressed because still failing* from *suppressed on a backoff earned by an already-resolved condition*.
- [ ] Backoff still lengthens under sustained failure — a recovery signal that is itself unreliable must not defeat the protection.
- [ ] A test drives a repo to a capped multiplier, signals recovery, and asserts the next run is scheduled ahead of the un-recovered schedule — failing against the current `Math.pow(2, consecutiveFailures)` implementation.
- [ ] **Restart-safety witness.** A process restart between the earned backoff and the next sweep neither zeroes `consecutiveFailures` nor synthesises a recovery. The test restarts across the boundary and asserts the durable streak and the retained cause both survive — the failure mode a literal gate adoption would have introduced.
- [ ] The recovery episode receipt is durable, and a due-bypass is granted only to repos whose retained cause belongs to that episode — a healthy canary does not blanket-release repos that failed for an unrelated reason.

## Out of Scope

- Making ingestion survive a slow embedding provider — sibling lane, and the reason these repos failed at all.
- KB healthcheck's embedding probe — sibling lane.
- The two remaining `boundedRetryGate` poles beyond this one (the backfill in infinite retry). Adopting this pole does not oblige the other.
- Changing the configured cadence or cap values.

## Avoided Traps

- **Lowering the cap.** Treats the symptom and weakens the protection that is otherwise working correctly. The cap is not the defect; the absence of a resumption condition is.
- **Resetting the counter on any readiness signal.** `accessReadiness` was `ready 4/4` throughout the outage — it measures repo access, not the embedding dependency that was actually failing. A resumption trigger wired to the wrong readiness surface would have re-armed all four repos every sweep for thirteen failures, converting a backoff into a retry storm against a struggling provider. The resumption condition must be tied to the dependency that earned the backoff.
- **Hand-rolling the resumption.** The primitive exists, names this consumer, and has a spec encoding its concurrency floor. A second implementation of bounded-retry-with-reason is how the notion got independently discovered three times in the first place.
- **Literal gate adoption — rejected on a source falsifier.** Making `boundedRetryGate` the sync scheduler regresses durable, restart-surviving per-repo backoff into process-local state, or stands up a second competing backoff authority. The primitive is right for *probe cadence*; it was never right for the *durable schedule*. See the corrected Fix above.
- **Wiring resumption to `accessReadiness`.** It measures git access and read `ready 4/4` throughout the embedding outage — it would have re-armed all four repos on every sweep for thirteen consecutive failures, converting a backoff into a retry storm against an already-struggling provider.

- 2026-08-08T17:49:10Z @tobiu referenced in commit `8818af7` - "feat(ai): a late embedding defers the ingest run instead of failing it (#16690) (#16713)

* feat(ai): a failed embed defers by default, because the observed code was unclassified (#16690)

An embed failure decides the fate of a whole ingest run. `classifyEmbedDisposition`
splits that decision into `deferrable` and `rejected`, with deferral as the DEFAULT
and rejection as a closed set of our own deliberate refusals.

The inverse — defer only on a recognised-transient allow-list — reads as the careful
design and would not have fired on the failure that motivated this. The deployment
reported `KB_VECTOR_EMBED_FAILED`, which is the UNCLASSIFIED sentinel: the provider's
code matched no entry in either vocabulary. A transient-allow-list rejects precisely
the specimen it was built to survive, and silently, because an unrecognised code looks
like a decision rather than a gap.

The asymmetry settles the default. Wrongly deferring a permanent failure costs bounded
retries whose backlog is observable as a pending depth that never falls. Wrongly failing
a merely-slow one discards the run's completed parse and chunk work — four repos at
thirteen consecutive failures with an empty collection.

Mutation-proved both directions: the allow-list design fails the specimen, composition,
non-vacuity and totality tests; unconditional deferral fails the rejected-set and
non-vacuity tests.

* feat(ai): deferral is opt-in by embed DOMAIN, because the summary stream is mixed (#16690)

`classifyEmbedDisposition` defaults to `deferrable`, which is correct within its
documented domain — an unrecognised EMBED failure must not discard a corpus, since
the code the production deployment actually reported was the unclassified sentinel.

Applied to an ingestion summary it would be a defect. That stream is mixed: 14
distinct `errors.push` sites in `IngestionService`, only two of which are the embed
path. Parse failures and tenant-guard rejections routed through the disposition
alone would defer forever — never failing, never advancing, never surfacing a
cause. Silently stuck is worse than loudly broken, and it would have been a new
bug introduced by the fix for an old one.

So deferral is opt-in by DOMAIN and default WITHIN it. `isEmbedFailureCode` is the
boundary the disposition deliberately does not police, keeping that function total
over its documented input while the consumer guards the mixed stream.

The domain set is derived from this module's own three sources rather than restated
beside them, so adding a provider mapping widens it in the same edit. A spec drives
`classifyEmbedFailureCode` over real inputs and asserts every emitted code is in the
domain — a hand-maintained list would have been one rename from silently refusing
deferral to a code that classifies fine.

Mutation-proved: dropping the domain check reds the mixed-stream test.

* fix(ai): a late embedding defers the run, it no longer fails it (#16690)

`assertErrorFreeIngestionSummary` had two outcomes and needed three. Any error
failed the whole run, so one slow embedding discarded the checkpoint for every
chunk that DID embed, the repo took a backoff step, and the corpus never grew.
Measured on an external deployment: four repos at consecutiveFailures 13, cadence
pinned to its cap, count 0. The parse and chunk work of every one of those runs
was thrown away because the tail of it was late.

`classifyIngestionOutcome` adds `deferred` — incomplete, not failed. The caller
holds the checkpoint, leaves consecutiveFailures neither incremented nor reset,
and advances lastRunAttemptAt so the lane returns at base cadence instead of
climbing toward the cap. Nothing is lost by waiting: VectorService never
re-embeds a chunk whose content-derived id is already present, so a later run
resumes rather than restarts.

Deferral is opt-in by DOMAIN and default within it, and the `every` is the whole
safety argument. A summary carries parse failures and tenant-guard rejections
alongside embed failures. One rejected code, one non-embed error, or one error
with no code at all fails the run exactly as before — deferring a permanently
malformed file would be silently stuck, which is worse than loudly broken.

Deferrals are counted separately in the cycle summary. Without that a sweep
deferring every repo reports "1 completed, 0 failed" and reads as a clean cycle,
which is the same empty-is-not-success defect this ticket family exists to close.

Two specs that drove the failure path with the deferrable KB_VECTOR_EMBED_FAILED
now use a rejected code, so the failure contract stays pinned for the case it
still governs rather than being deleted.

Mutation-proved: forcing `deferrable = false` reds the new deferred-outcome spec.

* fix(ai): a deferral arms the shared recovery episode, and an all-deferred sweep is not clean (#16690)

Composes this lane with the merged #16692 recovery path and answers all three

- 2026-08-21T21:58:33Z @tobiu referenced in commit `bbc98f6` - "fix(ai): the embedding recovery probe exercises the size that kills it (#17337) (#17490)

* fix(ai): the embedding recovery probe exercises the size that kills it (#17337)

The probe sent a 44-byte constant while production inputs ran to ~14,000
tokens, and peak memory for one non-causal embedding request scales with the
SQUARE of its token count. So it certified a property nobody asked about --
whether the HTTP plane answers at all -- while the property under question went
unmeasured. Its healthy verdict is what the tenant sweep consults to decide the
lane has recovered, so every green re-dispatched the batch that killed the
engine: 36 restarts, three repositories backoff-suppressed, and failureStreak 0
reported two seconds after the sweep's own lastErrorAt.

The input is now derived from the lane's admitted band, resolved at the use site
from the embedding leaves and injected into a pure builder, so embeddingProbe
stays Neo-free. At the shipped geometry that is 5,309 estimate-tokens against a
21,238-token band -- 354x the constant it replaces.

A quarter of the band rather than all of it, because a ceiling-sized cadence
probe would itself starve the lane: ~16.45 GiB marginal at the killing size,
scaling with n squared. What makes a fraction honest is that the probe reports
it. probeEstimateTokens, probeBandFraction and probeSized travel on every
verdict including healthy, and onto the public snapshot, so a consumer reads
"healthy at 25% of the admitted band" rather than "healthy".

An unresolvable band still probes and says it probed unsized. Refusing would
remove a signal; probing silently at marker size would rebuild the defect.

ECONNRESET, EPIPE, UND_ERR_SOCKET and ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE now classify as
provider-died rather than provider-failure. A connection that never came up is
ambient; a request accepted by a process that then went away is what an OOM kill
leaves behind, and it is the one observation this probe exists to make.

* fix(ai): scope the probe-size block to callers that ask for it (#17337)

The shared probe has three other consumers I did not sweep before changing its
return shape, and CI found one: memory-core's embedding write canary pins the
exact payload with toEqual.

The fix is not to update that assertion. Those consumers are healthcheck WRITE
CANARIES -- deliberately liveness-only, deliberately tiny, and not read as
readiness for real work, which is the distinction the ticket itself draws about
the container healthcheck. Emitting coverage fields as nulls there would change
two other services' public health contracts to describe a size they never
claimed to exercise.

So the block is absent unless a caller supplies probeSize, and the surface that
IS consumed as readiness -- the tenant recovery probe's bridge projection --
declares the fields explicitly. Absence is a reading exactly where a reading is
owed, and nowhere else.

* fix(ai): the probe's coverage actually reaches the surface that declares it (#17337)

@neo-gpt found three permanently-empty fields passing green CI.
buildEmbeddingProbeBlock produced probeEstimateTokens / probeBandFraction /
probeSized, and the bridge summarizer declared them -- and
getEmbeddingRecoveryProbeSnapshot between them projects an explicit ALLOWLIST
that did not include them. Both ends were right; the wire was never connected.

A verdict that reports its coverage as absent, always, is worse than one that
does not report coverage at all: it looks answered.

My arms could not have caught it. They tested the producer and they tested the
bridge fixture, each in isolation, so the hop where the drop happened had no
coverage -- and the handwritten no-size bridge fixture only ever exercised the
default arm. Reverting the projection left all seventeen of them green.

One exported projectProbeCoverage now serves every hop, so the three keys are
read from one place instead of being written at two ends and dropped between.
The new arm drives the real snapshot getter, and reverting the projection
reddens it -- which is the difference between fixing this and appearing to.

Remaining from that review and not in this commit: RA-1 (recovery eligibility
still authorizes a full re-dispatch from status alone, ignoring the coverage it
now receives) and RA-3 (Fix item 4's disposition). Both are mine and next.

* fix(ai): the recovery probe covers the work it authorizes (#17337)

RA-1, partially. The recovery verdict re-dispatches the whole awaiting cohort,
and a quarter-band probe never bounded that work.

Fork (a) as I described it to the reviewer is not implementable: the recovery
call site has episodeId and lastConsumedGenerationId and nothing else -- no
largest-chunk or max-input measure exists anywhere in the checkpoint or the KB
services. I priced that option without checking its precondition, which is a
correction I owe the review.

What IS available is the band ceiling, which dominates every admitted input. So
the recovery probe runs at fraction 1 while the cadence default stays 0.25 --
the two call sites answer different questions, and the ticket's Avoided Trap
against a full-ceiling probe is scoped to cadence, which this is not. If the
engine dies at full band, that is the probe finally failing the way the workload
fails: one classified request instead of the batch that killed it 36 times.

The eligibility check now reads coverage as well as status, asserted at the
decision rather than only at the call site, so a future fraction change stalls
recovery visibly instead of silently over-authorizing again.

EVIDENCE STATE, precisely: the guard is proven PRESENT -- the existing #16692
recovery arm went red until its stub carried full coverage, which is how I know
it is on the real path. It is not yet proven GUARDING: that arm is a positive
control and passes with the guard removed. The negative arm -- partial coverage
through runTask, asserting no bypass generation is minted -- is owed, and RA-1
stays STILL_OPEN until it exists.

Two arms I wrote for this and deleted rather than shipped: both asserted my own
predicate against literal objects and passed with the call site and the guard
both reverted. An arm that cannot fail is worse than no arm, and I had just
been corrected for exactly that one commit earlier.

* fix(ai): the full-band recovery probe gets a viable deadline and one death (#17337)

All three of the reviewer's source claims verified and all three were right.

EMBEDDING_RECOVERY_PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS is 30s while the incident's 13,980-token
request took ~180s. I quadrupled the probe and never touched its deadline, so a
HEALTHY full-band lane would report consumer-probe-timeout on exactly the
recovery this exists to detect. The deadline now travels with the size, derived
from the incident's own ~12.9 ms/token with a 1.5x drift margin; the caller's
value becomes a floor. 21,238 tokens buys 411s.

probeEmbeddingRecovery omitted maxFailureStreak, so the gate inherited Infinity
and a provider-died full-band probe would repeat at 30s->10m backoff forever.
The docblock I wrote beside the sizing claimed "one request" and the mechanism
said otherwise -- this ticket's own defect, written into its fix. Death is now
recorded against the proof identity and not re-attempted; ambient failures keep
the ordinary bounded retry, because a connection that never came up is cheap to
re-ask and refusing it would strand recovery.

The gate key carries the geometry. A cached quarter-band healthy cannot answer a
full-band question, and a key omitting the bound let it -- RA-1 one layer along.

STILL OWED, named rather than implied: the negative coverage-guard arm through
runTask; a slow-success control for the deadline (the computed value has no seam
a spec can observe); and a geometry-rotation control for the key.

The death arm took two corrections before it discriminated. Written naively it
re-asked inside the backoff window, where the gate's own TTL suppresses the call
-- so it proved the gate and said nothing about the bound. It now advances past
the window, exactly as its ambient control does, so the two differ only in
classification. Third arm today I caught passing without proving anything.

* fix(ai): the suite priced the full-band recovery probe, and it blocks the sweep (#17337)

Withdrawing two things I shipped an hour ago, both for reasons the suite found
and neither of us had.

The full-band recovery probe: the sweep AWAITS it. The same runTask arm passes
in 12.7s at a quarter band and exceeds 30s at the full one -- a held lease
against a dead provider, in production. So neither published fork survives
contact: the cheap probe does not bound the authorization it grants, and the
bounding probe blocks the sweep that needs it. The shape that works is one
neither fork described -- obtain the full-size proof OUT of the critical path
and let eligibility consume it -- and that is a design decision, open on the PR.

The size-derived deadline: correct in isolation and wrong in composition. A 30s
ceiling under a full-band probe makes a HEALTHY lane report a timeout, which is
the reviewer's finding and stands. But scaling it to 411s means the sweep blocks
for seven minutes. The third answer is not a number: the deadline is bounded by
what the CALLER can afford, which is the lease budget, not by what the request
needs.

Both defects are named in place rather than left as clean-looking code, because
the next reader will otherwise re-derive the same two dead ends.

KEPT, both green and both mutation-proven: death is recorded against the proof
identity and not re-attempted while ambient failures keep the ordinary retry;
and the gate key carries the geometry, so a cached quarter-band proof cannot
answer a full-band question.

* fix(ai): the recovery gate key named the PREVIOUS probe's band, not the one it admits (#17337)

My last commit here claimed "the gate key carries the geometry, so a cached
quarter-band proof cannot answer a full-band question", and called it
mutation-proven. The claim was false and the mutation could not have caught it.

The geometry was assigned inside `embeddingRecoveryProbeFn` and read when the
gate key was built -- one call earlier. The gate rotates a FRESH generation on
any key change (clean streak, empty cache, no backoff), so:

  call 1  key ...:pending:...   probe runs, provider DIES, death recorded there
  call 2  key ...:3034:0.25:... different identity -> death record unreachable,
                                 backoff discarded, the killing request fires
                                 again at the lane it just killed

That is the exact loop this ticket exists to stop, written into its own fix. The
"ONE destructive attempt per proof identity" bound was broken on the first death.

The two existing arms pass either way, which is why nothing caught it: they
inject `runProbe`, and the geometry was assigned inside the branch injection
replaces -- so the spec held one key forever while production moved it after
every run. Verifying the mechanism fired is not verifying the claim about it.

Fix: resolve `probeSize` once in `probeEmbeddingRecovery`, before the key, and
use it for both the key and the probe. Identity is now a function of config and
episodes alone. `sized` -- the builder's own word for an unresolvable band --
replaces inferring absence from a null fraction.

This is also the red CI: `lint-config-template-ssot` flagged the `?? 'pending'`
as a hidden-default beside an AiConfig read. The rule is line-scoped and the
`??` guarded an instance field, so it read as a false positive; it was pointing
at a real ordering defect. The guard is untouched.

New arm asserts the identity directly and is mutation-verified in the
discriminating direction: restoring the lagging read fails it while both
existing arms stay green."

- 2026-08-25T15:41:16Z @dawesi referenced in commit `04be5d1` - "feat(ai): a late embedding defers the ingest run instead of failing it (#16690) (#16713)

* feat(ai): a failed embed defers by default, because the observed code was unclassified (#16690)

An embed failure decides the fate of a whole ingest run. `classifyEmbedDisposition`
splits that decision into `deferrable` and `rejected`, with deferral as the DEFAULT
and rejection as a closed set of our own deliberate refusals.

The inverse — defer only on a recognised-transient allow-list — reads as the careful
design and would not have fired on the failure that motivated this. The deployment
reported `KB_VECTOR_EMBED_FAILED`, which is the UNCLASSIFIED sentinel: the provider's
code matched no entry in either vocabulary. A transient-allow-list rejects precisely
the specimen it was built to survive, and silently, because an unrecognised code looks
like a decision rather than a gap.

The asymmetry settles the default. Wrongly deferring a permanent failure costs bounded
retries whose backlog is observable as a pending depth that never falls. Wrongly failing
a merely-slow one discards the run's completed parse and chunk work — four repos at
thirteen consecutive failures with an empty collection.

Mutation-proved both directions: the allow-list design fails the specimen, composition,
non-vacuity and totality tests; unconditional deferral fails the rejected-set and
non-vacuity tests.

* feat(ai): deferral is opt-in by embed DOMAIN, because the summary stream is mixed (#16690)

`classifyEmbedDisposition` defaults to `deferrable`, which is correct within its
documented domain — an unrecognised EMBED failure must not discard a corpus, since
the code the production deployment actually reported was the unclassified sentinel.

Applied to an ingestion summary it would be a defect. That stream is mixed: 14
distinct `errors.push` sites in `IngestionService`, only two of which are the embed
path. Parse failures and tenant-guard rejections routed through the disposition
alone would defer forever — never failing, never advancing, never surfacing a
cause. Silently stuck is worse than loudly broken, and it would have been a new
bug introduced by the fix for an old one.

So deferral is opt-in by DOMAIN and default WITHIN it. `isEmbedFailureCode` is the
boundary the disposition deliberately does not police, keeping that function total
over its documented input while the consumer guards the mixed stream.

The domain set is derived from this module's own three sources rather than restated
beside them, so adding a provider mapping widens it in the same edit. A spec drives
`classifyEmbedFailureCode` over real inputs and asserts every emitted code is in the
domain — a hand-maintained list would have been one rename from silently refusing
deferral to a code that classifies fine.

Mutation-proved: dropping the domain check reds the mixed-stream test.

* fix(ai): a late embedding defers the run, it no longer fails it (#16690)

`assertErrorFreeIngestionSummary` had two outcomes and needed three. Any error
failed the whole run, so one slow embedding discarded the checkpoint for every
chunk that DID embed, the repo took a backoff step, and the corpus never grew.
Measured on an external deployment: four repos at consecutiveFailures 13, cadence
pinned to its cap, count 0. The parse and chunk work of every one of those runs
was thrown away because the tail of it was late.

`classifyIngestionOutcome` adds `deferred` — incomplete, not failed. The caller
holds the checkpoint, leaves consecutiveFailures neither incremented nor reset,
and advances lastRunAttemptAt so the lane returns at base cadence instead of
climbing toward the cap. Nothing is lost by waiting: VectorService never
re-embeds a chunk whose content-derived id is already present, so a later run
resumes rather than restarts.

Deferral is opt-in by DOMAIN and default within it, and the `every` is the whole
safety argument. A summary carries parse failures and tenant-guard rejections
alongside embed failures. One rejected code, one non-embed error, or one error
with no code at all fails the run exactly as before — deferring a permanently
malformed file would be silently stuck, which is worse than loudly broken.

Deferrals are counted separately in the cycle summary. Without that a sweep
deferring every repo reports "1 completed, 0 failed" and reads as a clean cycle,
which is the same empty-is-not-success defect this ticket family exists to close.

Two specs that drove the failure path with the deferrable KB_VECTOR_EMBED_FAILED
now use a rejected code, so the failure contract stays pinned for the case it
still governs rather than being deleted.

Mutation-proved: forcing `deferrable = false` reds the new deferred-outcome spec.

* fix(ai): a deferral arms the shared recovery episode, and an all-deferred sweep is not clean (#16690)

Composes this lane with the merged #16692 recovery path and answers all three
review RAs from @neo-gpt.

The collision the merge exposed: his recovery episode armed on a FAILURE carrying
a bounded embedding cause, and this lane makes exactly those codes defer instead
of fail — removing his trigger. His call was (a): a deferrable outcome is
recovery-eligible on the same terms, because it proves precisely what the canary
measures, no checkpoint progress against the embedding dependency. Giving deferral
its own episode kind would fork the resumption authority in two.

So `buildEmbeddingRecoveryAfterFailure` is generalized to
`buildEmbeddingRecoveryEpisode` — both a failure and a deferral advance the SAME
episode, a consumed generation folds to lastConsumedGenerationId/At, and a newly
healthy canary generation is required before another bypass. A still-starved
provider cannot buy one retry per sweep by deferring rather than failing.

RA-1: deferral preserves `consecutiveFailures` exactly, neither incremented nor
reset, and adds no cadence exception. The retained streak still governs and the
recovery generation is the single resumption authority. The earlier "returns at
base cadence" claim was false for the production specimen at streak 13, where
isRepoDue multiplies by 8192; the old cohort could not catch it because every repo
started at 0, where the multiplier is 1.

RA-2: `attemptedCount` excluded deferrals, so an all-deferred sweep took the
"every repo was not-due" branch and reported `completed` — the same
empty-is-not-success defect this family exists to close. It now reports `deferred`,
which routes to markSkipped so lastSuccessAt does not advance on a cycle that
ingested nothing.

Ordering fix: `classifyEmbeddingRecoveryState` read the failure count before
recovery, returning null for a repo that deferred at streak 0 while owning a real
episode — the one repo actually waiting on the canary. Recovery is inspected
first; the failure count now only decides the ordinary-backoff case.

The deferred projection also publishes `recoveryState`, so the state that is
waiting on the canary is not the only one whose classification is invisible.

141 focused tests green. New specimens: capped-streak deferral arms and re-uses
one episode without moving the streak, and an all-deferred sweep is not clean."
